claim: Apical PAR complex proteins PAR-6/Par6 and PKC-3/aPkc remained apical during mitosis in the developing C. elegans intestine.
source: Live imaging revealed that apical PAR complex proteins PAR-6/Par6 and PKC-3/aPkc remained apical during mitosis while apical microtubules and microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) proteins were transiently removed.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data presented in the manuscript showing PAR-6 and PKC-3 localization during mitosis.

claim: Apical microtubules and microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) proteins were transiently removed during mitosis in the developing C. elegans intestine.
source: Live imaging revealed that apical PAR complex proteins PAR-6/Par6 and PKC-3/aPkc remained apical during mitosis while apical microtubules and microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) proteins were transiently removed.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data showing MTOC protein removal during mitosis.

claim: Intestine-specific depletion of PAR-6 caused persistent gaps in the apical MTOC after cell division.
source: Intestine-specific depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, and the aPkc regulator CDC-42/Cdc42 caused persistent gaps in the apical MTOC as well as in other apical and junctional proteins after cell division and in non-dividing cells that elongated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from intestine-specific protein depletion experiments.

claim: Intestine-specific depletion of PKC-3 caused persistent gaps in the apical MTOC after cell division.
source: Intestine-specific depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, and the aPkc regulator CDC-42/Cdc42 caused persistent gaps in the apical MTOC as well as in other apical and junctional proteins after cell division and in non-dividing cells that elongated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from intestine-specific protein depletion experiments.

claim: Intestine-specific depletion of CDC-42/Cdc42 caused persistent gaps in the apical MTOC after cell division.
source: Intestine-specific depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, and the aPkc regulator CDC-42/Cdc42 caused persistent gaps in the apical MTOC as well as in other apical and junctional proteins after cell division and in non-dividing cells that elongated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from intestine-specific protein depletion experiments.

claim: Intestine-specific depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, and CDC-42 caused gaps in apical and junctional proteins in non-dividing cells that elongated.
source: Intestine-specific depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, and the aPkc regulator CDC-42/Cdc42 caused persistent gaps in the apical MTOC as well as in other apical and junctional proteins after cell division and in non-dividing cells that elongated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing gaps in elongating non-dividing cells.

claim: Gaps in apical and junctional proteins coincided with luminal constrictions that blocked food upon hatching.
source: Upon hatching, gaps coincided with luminal constrictions that blocked food, and larvae arrested and died.
evidence: Supported by feeding assay data showing food blockage at sites of luminal constrictions.

claim: Larvae with intestine-specific depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, and CDC-42 arrested and died upon hatching.
source: Upon hatching, gaps coincided with luminal constrictions that blocked food, and larvae arrested and died.
evidence: Supported by larval arrest assay data.

claim: The apical PAR complex maintains apical and junctional continuity to construct a functional intestinal tube.
source: Thus, the apical PAR complex maintains apical and junctional continuity to construct a functional intestinal tube.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Epithelial cells polarize along an apicobasal axis, collectively positioning their apical surfaces facing outward.
source: Epithelial cells polarize along an apicobasal axis, collectively positioning their apical surfaces facing outward with important specializations such as microvilli and cilia, while their basolateral domains contact neighboring cells and basement membranes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epithelial cell polarity.

claim: Junctional complexes form belt-like bands at the cell periphery that adhere neighboring cells together and separate the apical and basolateral domains.
source: Junctional complexes ('junctions') form belt-like bands at the cell periphery that adhere neighboring cells together and separate the apical and basolateral domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epithelial junctions, supported by citation to Pickett et al., 2019.

claim: In most epithelial cells, cell division physically cleaves their polarized domains and daughters must build junctions at the new cell-cell contact while maintaining correct apicobasal polarity.
source: In most epithelial cells, cell division physically cleaves their polarized domains and daughters must build junctions at the new cell-cell contact while maintaining correct apicobasal polarity (Le Bras and Le Borgne, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Le Bras and Le Borgne, 2014.

claim: In many interphase epithelial cells, microtubules are arranged in parallel arrays emanating from an apically localized microtubule-organizing center (MTOC).
source: In many interphase epithelial cells, such as Caenorhabditis elegans and mammalian intestinal cells, Drosophila tracheal and follicle cells, and many mammalian epithelial cell lines, microtubules are arranged in parallel arrays emanating from an apically localized microtubule-organizing center (MTOC), allowing for intracellular vesicle transport and apicobasal polarity maintenance (Sanchez and Feldman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanchez and Feldman, 2017.

claim: During mitosis, microtubules are temporarily rearranged into radial arrays around the centrosomal MTOC and then returned to the apical surface.
source: During mitosis, microtubules are temporarily rearranged into radial arrays around the centrosomal MTOC and then returned to the apical surface (Pease and Tirnauer, 2011; Yang and Feldman, 2015), yet how microtubules are released from and returned to the apical surface is unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to Pease and Tirnauer, 2011 and Yang and Feldman, 2015.

claim: How microtubules are released from and returned to the apical surface during mitosis is unknown.
source: During mitosis, microtubules are temporarily rearranged into radial arrays around the centrosomal MTOC and then returned to the apical surface (Pease and Tirnauer, 2011; Yang and Feldman, 2015), yet how microtubules are released from and returned to the apical surface is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The apical PAR polarity complex can play important roles in epithelial cell remodeling by orienting the mitotic spindle during mitosis.
source: The highly conserved apical PAR polarity complex can play important roles in epithelial cell remodeling by, for example, orienting the mitotic spindle during mitosis (Kuchinke et al., 1998; Mack and Georgiou, 2014; Hao et al., 2010; Siegrist and Doe, 2005) and regulating actin dynamics during apical constriction (David et al., 2010; Ishiuchi and Takeichi, 2011; Walck-Shannon et al., 2016; Zilberman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuchinke et al., 1998; Mack and Georgiou, 2014; Hao et al., 2010; Siegrist and Doe, 2005.

claim: The apical PAR polarity complex can play important roles in epithelial cell remodeling by regulating actin dynamics during apical constriction.
source: The highly conserved apical PAR polarity complex can play important roles in epithelial cell remodeling by, for example, orienting the mitotic spindle during mitosis (Kuchinke et al., 1998; Mack and Georgiou, 2014; Hao et al., 2010; Siegrist and Doe, 2005) and regulating actin dynamics during apical constriction (David et al., 2010; Ishiuchi and Takeichi, 2011; Walck-Shannon et al., 2016; Zilberman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to David et al., 2010; Ishiuchi and Takeichi, 2011; Walck-Shannon et al., 2016; Zilberman et al., 2017.

claim: The PAR complex consists of PAR-3/Par3, PAR-6/Par6, PKC-3/aPkc, and CDC-42/Cdc42.
source: This 'PAR complex,' consisting of PAR-3/Par3, PAR-6/Par6, PKC-3/aPkc, and CDC-42/Cdc42, is best characterized for its role in the formation and maintenance of apicobasal domains and junctions in many tissues and organisms (Pickett et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PAR complex composition, supported by citation to Pickett et al., 2019.

claim: The PAR complex is best characterized for its role in the formation and maintenance of apicobasal domains and junctions in many tissues and organisms.
source: This 'PAR complex,' consisting of PAR-3/Par3, PAR-6/Par6, PKC-3/aPkc, and CDC-42/Cdc42, is best characterized for its role in the formation and maintenance of apicobasal domains and junctions in many tissues and organisms (Pickett et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pickett et al., 2019.

claim: The scaffold Par6 binds the kinase aPkc.
source: The scaffold Par6 binds the kinase aPkc; another scaffold Par3 recruits them to the apical surface, and the Rho-family GTPase Cdc42 replaces Par3 and activates aPkc kinase activity (Achilleos et al., 2010; Harris and Peifer, 2005; Hutterer et al., 2004; Joberty et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2000; Rodriguez et al., 2017; Totong et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Par3 recruits Par6 and aPkc to the apical surface.
source: The scaffold Par6 binds the kinase aPkc; another scaffold Par3 recruits them to the apical surface, and the Rho-family GTPase Cdc42 replaces Par3 and activates aPkc kinase activity (Achilleos et al., 2010; Harris and Peifer, 2005; Hutterer et al., 2004; Joberty et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2000; Rodriguez et al., 2017; Totong et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cdc42 replaces Par3 and activates aPkc kinase activity.
source: The scaffold Par6 binds the kinase aPkc; another scaffold Par3 recruits them to the apical surface, and the Rho-family GTPase Cdc42 replaces Par3 and activates aPkc kinase activity (Achilleos et al., 2010; Harris and Peifer, 2005; Hutterer et al., 2004; Joberty et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2000; Rodriguez et al., 2017; Totong et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: aPkc phosphorylates and removes basolateral proteins from the apical domain.
source: aPkc phosphorylates and removes basolateral proteins from the apical domain, and mutual inhibition between apical and basolateral proteins maintains and refines the apical and basolateral domains (Pickett et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pickett et al., 2019.

claim: Mutual inhibition between apical and basolateral proteins maintains and refines the apical and basolateral domains.
source: aPkc phosphorylates and removes basolateral proteins from the apical domain, and mutual inhibition between apical and basolateral proteins maintains and refines the apical and basolateral domains (Pickett et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pickett et al., 2019.

claim: The PAR complex promotes adherens junction plasticity, tight junction formation, and junction maintenance.
source: The PAR complex also promotes adherens junction plasticity, tight junction formation, and junction maintenance (Georgiou et al., 2008; Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Rusu and Georgiou, 2020; Totong et al., 2007; Wallace et al., 2010; Zilberman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: PAR-3 is required to establish the apical domain of intestinal cells along a shared central midline in early C. elegans embryonic intestinal development.
source: PAR-3 is required to establish the apical domain of intestinal cells along a shared central midline, which later forms the lumen, and to recruit other PAR complex proteins and microtubules to the apical surface (Achilleos et al., 2010; Feldman and Priess, 2012); PAR-6 and PKC-3 localize interdependently to the apical surface, and PAR-6 is required for junction formation but not polarity (Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Totong et al., 2007); and CDC-42 is not required for polarity or junction formation (Zilberman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Achilleos et al., 2010; Feldman and Priess, 2012.

claim: PAR-3 recruits other PAR complex proteins and microtubules to the apical surface in early C. elegans embryonic intestinal development.
source: PAR-3 is required to establish the apical domain of intestinal cells along a shared central midline, which later forms the lumen, and to recruit other PAR complex proteins and microtubules to the apical surface (Achilleos et al., 2010; Feldman and Priess, 2012); PAR-6 and PKC-3 localize interdependently to the apical surface, and PAR-6 is required for junction formation but not polarity (Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Totong et al., 2007); and CDC-42 is not required for polarity or junction formation (Zilberman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Achilleos et al., 2010; Feldman and Priess, 2012.

claim: PAR-6 and PKC-3 localize interdependently to the apical surface in early C. elegans embryonic intestinal development.
source: PAR-3 is required to establish the apical domain of intestinal cells along a shared central midline, which later forms the lumen, and to recruit other PAR complex proteins and microtubules to the apical surface (Achilleos et al., 2010; Feldman and Priess, 2012); PAR-6 and PKC-3 localize interdependently to the apical surface, and PAR-6 is required for junction formation but not polarity (Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Totong et al., 2007); and CDC-42 is not required for polarity or junction formation (Zilberman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Totong et al., 2007.

claim: PAR-6 is required for junction formation but not polarity in early C. elegans embryonic intestinal development.
source: PAR-3 is required to establish the apical domain of intestinal cells along a shared central midline, which later forms the lumen, and to recruit other PAR complex proteins and microtubules to the apical surface (Achilleos et al., 2010; Feldman and Priess, 2012); PAR-6 and PKC-3 localize interdependently to the apical surface, and PAR-6 is required for junction formation but not polarity (Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Totong et al., 2007); and CDC-42 is not required for polarity or junction formation (Zilberman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Totong et al., 2007.

claim: CDC-42 is not required for polarity or junction formation in early C. elegans embryonic intestinal development.
source: PAR-3 is required to establish the apical domain of intestinal cells along a shared central midline, which later forms the lumen, and to recruit other PAR complex proteins and microtubules to the apical surface (Achilleos et al., 2010; Feldman and Priess, 2012); PAR-6 and PKC-3 localize interdependently to the apical surface, and PAR-6 is required for junction formation but not polarity (Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Totong et al., 2007); and CDC-42 is not required for polarity or junction formation (Zilberman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zilberman et al., 2017.

claim: The 16-cell primordial C. elegans intestine (E16) is arranged into two tiers of 10 dorsal and 6 ventral cells.
source: The 16-cell primordial intestine (E16) is arranged into two tiers of 10 dorsal and 6 ventral cells.
evidence: This is a description of C. elegans intestinal anatomy.

claim: C. elegans intestinal cells begin to polarize soon after they are born, building a continuous apical domain along a central midline, the future lumen.
source: These cells begin to polarize soon after they are born, building a continuous apical domain along a central midline, the future lumen (Leung et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leung et al., 1999.

claim: Adherens and septate-like junctions form a single 'apical junction' that localizes around the apical domain between left/right, dorsal/ventral, and anterior/posterior pairs of cells in a ladder-like arrangement along the midline in the C. elegans intestine.
source: Adherens and septate-like junctions form a single 'apical junction' that localizes around the apical domain between left/right, dorsal/ventral, and anterior/posterior pairs of cells in a ladder-like arrangement along the midline (Costa et al., 1998; Labouesse, 2006; Leung et al., 1999; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costa et al., 1998; Labouesse, 2006; Leung et al., 1999 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Two pairs of anterior and posterior cells ('star cells') undergo an additional round of mitosis after polarity is established in the C. elegans intestine.
source: Two pairs of anterior and posterior cells, referred to here as 'star cells,' undergo an additional round of mitosis after polarity is established while the other 12 'non-star cells' remain in interphase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The other 12 'non-star cells' remain in interphase while star cells divide in the C. elegans intestine.
source: Two pairs of anterior and posterior cells, referred to here as 'star cells,' undergo an additional round of mitosis after polarity is established while the other 12 'non-star cells' remain in interphase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The embryonic C. elegans intestine more than doubles its midline length from a polarized primordium at bean stage to the 1.5- to 1.8-fold stage.
source: The embryonic intestine more than doubles its midline length from a polarized primordium at bean stage to the 1.5- to 1.8-fold stage (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A–C showing intestinal elongation.

claim: C. elegans embryos hatch as L1 (first larval stage) larvae with a functional intestine.
source: Embryos hatch as L1 (first larval stage) larvae with a functional intestine (Figure 1C), built from a series of nine stacked 'int' rings with a continuous central hollow lumen through which food passes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The L1 larval C. elegans intestine is built from a series of nine stacked 'int' rings with a continuous central hollow lumen through which food passes.
source: Embryos hatch as L1 (first larval stage) larvae with a functional intestine (Figure 1C), built from a series of nine stacked 'int' rings with a continuous central hollow lumen through which food passes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Apical microtubules and the γ-Tubulin Ring Complex (γ-TuRC) transiently leave the apical surface when star cells divide and centrosomes are reactivated as MTOCs to build the mitotic spindle.
source: Apical microtubules and the microtubule nucleator γ-Tubulin Ring Complex (γ-TuRC) transiently leave the apical surface when star cells divide and centrosomes are reactivated as MTOCs to build the mitotic spindle (Pease and Tirnauer, 2011; Yang and Feldman, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pease and Tirnauer, 2011; Yang and Feldman, 2015.

claim: The loss of apical microtubules during star cell division creates a visible 'midline gap' in MTOC proteins as both the left and right cells reactivate centrosomal MTOCs.
source: The loss of apical microtubules is easiest to see when star cells divide at the same time. Both apical surfaces lose apical microtubules during mitosis, creating a visible 'midline gap' in MTOC proteins as both the left and right cells reactivate centrosomal MTOCs; the midline gap is then refilled upon mitotic exit (Figure 1D, E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C, F; Yang and Feldman, 2015).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1D, E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C, F and citation to Yang and Feldman, 2015.

claim: The midline gap in MTOC proteins is refilled upon mitotic exit.
source: The loss of apical microtubules is easiest to see when star cells divide at the same time. Both apical surfaces lose apical microtubules during mitosis, creating a visible 'midline gap' in MTOC proteins as both the left and right cells reactivate centrosomal MTOCs; the midline gap is then refilled upon mitotic exit (Figure 1D, E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C, F; Yang and Feldman, 2015).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1D, E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C, F and citation to Yang and Feldman, 2015.

claim: Microtubules, γ-TuRC components TBG-1/γ-tubulin and GIP-1/GCP3, and other MTOC and microtubule-associated proteins left the apical surface during mitosis.
source: In addition to microtubules and the γ-TuRC components TBG-1/γ-tubulin and GIP-1/GCP3, all other MTOC and microtubule-associated proteins we examined also left the apical surface during mitosis (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1E showing protein localization during mitosis.

claim: Some MTOC proteins (γ-TuRC, ZYG-9/chTOG, AIR-1/Aurora A) localized to the active centrosomes during mitosis.
source: Some MTOC proteins localized to the active centrosomes (γ-TuRC, ZYG-9/chTOG, AIR-1/Aurora A), while other proteins did not and likely became cytoplasmic (NOCA-1/Ninein, PTRN-1/CAMSAP, VAB-10B/Spectraplakin).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of protein localization during mitosis.

claim: Some MTOC proteins (NOCA-1/Ninein, PTRN-1/CAMSAP, VAB-10B/Spectraplakin) did not localize to active centrosomes and likely became cytoplasmic during mitosis.
source: Some MTOC proteins localized to the active centrosomes (γ-TuRC, ZYG-9/chTOG, AIR-1/Aurora A), while other proteins did not and likely became cytoplasmic (NOCA-1/Ninein, PTRN-1/CAMSAP, VAB-10B/Spectraplakin).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and inference about protein localization during mitosis.

claim: The observed removal of apical MTOC proteins during mitosis, including the MTOC anchoring proteins VAB-10B and WDR-62, suggests the complete inactivation of the apical surface as an MTOC.
source: The observed removal of apical MTOC proteins during mitosis, including the MTOC anchoring proteins VAB-10B and WDR-62 (Sanchez et al., 2020), suggests the complete inactivation of the apical surface as an MTOC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed removal of MTOC proteins, supported by citation to Sanchez et al., 2020.

claim: Junctional proteins retained some localization during mitosis, albeit reduced as compared with interphase neighboring cells.
source: Junctional proteins retained some localization during mitosis, albeit reduced as compared with interphase neighboring cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1F showing junctional protein localization during mitosis.

claim: Localization of the septate-like junction-associated protein DLG-1/Discs large was most strongly reduced during mitosis.
source: Localization of the septate-like junction-associated protein DLG-1/Discs large was most strongly reduced during mitosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D), and the adherens junction protein HMR-1/E-cadherin was also reduced compared to the non-dividing 'non-star' intestinal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, E), appearing as thin fluorescent threads as new cell boundaries formed.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D.

claim: The adherens junction protein HMR-1/E-cadherin was reduced during mitosis compared to the non-dividing 'non-star' intestinal cells, appearing as thin fluorescent threads as new cell boundaries formed.
source: Localization of the septate-like junction-associated protein DLG-1/Discs large was most strongly reduced during mitosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D), and the adherens junction protein HMR-1/E-cadherin was also reduced compared to the non-dividing 'non-star' intestinal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, E), appearing as thin fluorescent threads as new cell boundaries formed.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, E.

claim: ACT-5/actin and three members of the PAR complex PAR-3/Par3, PAR-6/Par6, and PKC-3/aPkc all remained apically localized during mitosis.
source: The other apical proteins examined, ACT-5/actin and three members of the PAR complex PAR-3/Par3, PAR-6/Par6, and PKC-3/aPkc, all remained apically localized during mitosis (Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, G).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, G.

claim: PAR complex proteins actively mark the apical surface during mitotic remodeling to return apical MTOC function after division.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that PAR complex proteins actively mark the apical surface during mitotic remodeling to return apical MTOC function after division, thereby restoring a continuous apical MTOC.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that PAR complex proteins remain apical during mitosis.

claim: In control embryos in which anterior star cells divided synchronously, a midline gap formed in the apical MTOC as centrosomes recruited additional TBG-1.
source: In control embryos in which anterior star cells divided synchronously, a midline gap formed in the apical MTOC as centrosomes recruited additional TBG-1; MTOC proteins returned and filled the gap within 12 min as the centrosomes inactivated and shed TBG-1 (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2E, F showing time-lapse imaging of MTOC during division.

claim: In control embryos, MTOC proteins returned and filled the gap within 12 min as the centrosomes inactivated and shed TBG-1.
source: In control embryos in which anterior star cells divided synchronously, a midline gap formed in the apical MTOC as centrosomes recruited additional TBG-1; MTOC proteins returned and filled the gap within 12 min as the centrosomes inactivated and shed TBG-1 (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2E, F showing time-lapse imaging of MTOC during division.

claim: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, midline MTOC gaps that formed during synchronous divisions persisted long after mitotic exit through the end of the time course, for a minimum of 24 min.
source: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, however, midline MTOC gaps that formed during synchronous divisions persisted long after mitotic exit through the end of the time course, for a minimum of 24 min (Figure 2E, G).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2E, G showing time-lapse imaging of MTOC in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.

claim: The persistence of the midline gap in MTOC proteins in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) embryos is consistent with the hypothesis that PAR complex proteins promote the return of apical MTOC function after division.
source: The persistence of the midline gap in MTOC proteins in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) embryos is consistent with our hypothesis that PAR complex proteins promote the return of apical MTOC function after division.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing persistent gaps in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) embryos.

claim: In elongating control intestines, the apical MTOC remained continuous along the midline in both star cell daughters and in non-star cells.
source: In elongating control intestines, the apical MTOC remained continuous along the midline in both star cell daughters and in non-star cells (Figure 3A, inset).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3A showing MTOC continuity in control intestines.

claim: In elongating PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines, midline gaps in MTOC proteins formed both in star cell daughters and in non-star cells that had not recently divided.
source: By contrast, in elongating PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines, midline gaps in MTOC proteins formed both in star cell daughters and in non-star cells that had not recently divided (Figure 3B, C, insets); the midline gaps were clearly visualized by line scans (Figure 3B', C').
evidence: Supported by Figure 3B, C showing gaps in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines.

claim: Only few PAR-6gut(-) embryos had small midline gaps in TBG-1 and PTRN-1 prior to the star cell divisions and elongation.
source: Consistent with elongation causing gaps to form, we observed only few PAR-6gut(-) embryos with small midline gaps in TBG-1 and PTRN-1 prior to the star cell divisions and elongation (control: n = 1/17, PAR-6gut(-): n = 5/29).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data comparing gap frequency before and after elongation.

claim: In control intestines, the apical MTOC stayed continuous as the average midline length increased approximately 80% in 50 min.
source: In control intestines, the apical MTOC stayed continuous as the average midline length increased approximately 80% in 50 min (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3D showing time-lapse imaging of control intestines.

claim: In PAR-6gut(-) intestines, the apical MTOC formed gaps as the average apical surface elongated 70% in 50 min.
source: In PAR-6gut(-) intestines, however, the apical MTOC formed gaps as the average apical surface elongated 70% in 50 min (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3E showing time-lapse imaging of PAR-6gut(-) intestines.

claim: 55.5% of PAR-6gut(-) and 44.4% of PKC-3gut(-) embryos had one or more gaps compared with 0% of control embryos.
source: By these stringent criteria, 55.5% of PAR-6gut(-) and 44.4% of PKC-3gut(-) embryos had one or more gaps compared with 0% of control embryos (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3F showing quantification of gaps.

claim: 4.1% of PAR-6gut(-) and 3.7% of PKC-3gut(-) midline measurements were background level compared to 0% in control intestines.
source: As a total proportion of the midline MTOC line scan signal, we found that 4.1% of PAR-6gut(-) and 3.7% of PKC-3gut(-) midline measurements were background level compared to 0% in control intestines (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3G showing quantification of background-level measurements.

claim: The number of background-level measurements increased over time in PAR-6gut(-) embryos but not in control embryos.
source: The number of background-level measurements increased over time in PAR-6gut(-) embryos but not in control embryos (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by Figure 3H showing paired comparisons over time.

claim: PAR-6 and PKC-3 are required for maintaining apical MTOC continuity between neighboring non-dividing cells during intestinal elongation.
source: These results suggest that in addition to their roles in promoting continuity in dividing cells, PAR-6 and PKC-3 are also required for maintaining apical MTOC continuity between neighboring non-dividing cells during intestinal elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of gaps in non-dividing cells during elongation.

claim: No physical separation between intestinal cells was detected in control, PAR-6gut(-), PKC-3gut(-), or CDC-42gut(-) embryos.
source: We did not detect physical separation between intestinal cells in control, PAR-6gut(-), PKC-3gut(-), or CDC-42gut(-) embryos (Figure 4A–F); the membrane marker clearly spanned the gaps in TBG-1 (Figure 4B–D insets), and neighboring intestinal cells remained adjacent to each other.
evidence: Supported by Figure 4A–F showing membrane marker spanning gaps.

claim: A higher frequency of gap formation was observed in the 8 star cells than in the 12 non-star cells in all three PAR complex depletion backgrounds.
source: With intestinal cell membranes marked, we could also map which cells formed gaps within the intestine, and we observed a higher frequency of gap formation in the 8 star cells than in the 12 non-star cells in all three PAR complex depletion backgrounds (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 4F showing gap frequency in star vs. non-star cells.

claim: Blocking star cell divisions with the cdc-25.2(0) mutation reduced the difference in gap frequency between star cells and non-star cells in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.
source: While midline gaps were more frequent in PAR-6gut(-) star cells than non-star cells (star: 31% vs. non-star: 15%, Figure 4I), this difference in gap frequency was abrogated in PAR-6gut(-); cdc-25.2(0) double mutant embryos (star: 8% vs. non-star:19%, Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by Figure 4I showing gap frequency in PAR-6gut(-) vs. PAR-6gut(-); cdc-25.2(0) embryos.

claim: PAR-6 is specifically required to protect MTOC continuity from disruption by cell division.
source: This result suggests that PAR-6 is specifically required to protect MTOC continuity from disruption by cell division.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cdc-25.2(0) experiment showing reduced gap frequency when divisions are blocked.

claim: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, apical YFP::ACT-5/actin formed gaps along the midline in both star cell daughters and in non-star cells.
source: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, apical YFP::ACT-5/actin formed gaps along the midline in both star cell daughters and in non-star cells (10/19 and 9/19 gaps, respectively; Figure 5A, B), similar to MTOC protein gaps (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5A, B showing ACT-5 gaps.

claim: Midline gaps in PAR-3::tagRFP overlapped with gaps in PTRN-1::GFP in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.
source: In addition, we found midline gaps in PAR-3::tagRFP, which normally localizes to the apical surface and junctions in the intestine (Achilleos et al., 2010; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), that overlapped with gaps in PTRN-1::GFP (Figure 5C, F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5C, F showing overlapping gaps in PAR-3 and PTRN-1.

claim: PAR-6 is essential for the general continuity of the apical domain during elongation.
source: These results suggest that PAR-6 is essential not only for a continuous apical MTOC but also for the general continuity of the apical domain during elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of gaps in multiple apical markers.

claim: 92% of TBG-1 gaps spanned the interface between adjacent cells in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.
source: Our analysis of GFP::CAAX in PAR-6gut(-) embryos revealed that 92% of TBG-1 gaps spanned the interface between adjacent cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 4F showing gap location analysis.

claim: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, HMR-1::GFP localized to the outer edge of the TBG-1 signal as expected for a junctional protein, but was generally absent from the TBG-1 midline gaps.
source: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, HMR-1::GFP localized to the outer edge of the TBG-1 signal as expected for a junctional protein, but was generally absent from the TBG-1 midline gaps (Figure 5D, F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5D, F showing HMR-1 localization relative to TBG-1 gaps.

claim: DLG-1 was clearly absent from most TBG-1 gaps in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.
source: We also examined DLG-1::mNG localization, which was severely perturbed along the entire midline in PAR-6gut(-) embryos as has previously been reported following PAR-6 depletion (Totong et al., 2007). We occasionally found large patches of DLG-1 that colocalized with TBG-1; however, DLG-1 was clearly absent from most TBG-1 gaps (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5E, F showing DLG-1 localization relative to TBG-1 gaps, and citation to Totong et al., 2007.

claim: Junctional complexes do not spread into and fill midline gaps in apical proteins following PAR-6 depletion.
source: Together, these results indicate that junctional complexes do not spread into and fill midline gaps in apical proteins following PAR-6 depletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that junctional proteins are absent from gaps.

claim: In control intestines, LGL-1::GFP and LET-413::GFP were observed at lateral surfaces and strongly reduced at the midline where apical markers TBG-1::mCherry and PAR-3::tagRFP localized.
source: In control intestines, LGL-1::GFP and LET-413::GFP were observed at lateral surfaces and strongly reduced at the midline where apical markers TBG-1::mCherry and PAR-3::tagRFP localized (Figure 5G–J).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5G–J showing LGL-1 and LET-413 localization in control intestines.

claim: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, LGL-1 and LET-413 signal intensities were significantly elevated in most gaps, and similar to intensities at lateral surfaces.
source: In PAR-6gut(-) embryos, LGL-1 and LET-413 signal intensities were significantly elevated in most gaps, and similar to intensities at lateral surfaces (Figure 5G–J).
evidence: Supported by Figure 5G–J showing LGL-1 and LET-413 localization in PAR-6gut(-) embryos.

claim: LGL-1 and LET-413 were also observed at midline 'non-gap' regions in PAR-6gut(-) embryos, where apical markers localized.
source: LGL-1 and LET-413 were also observed at midline 'non-gap' regions, where apical markers localized (Figure 5G, I insets, orange arrowheads), suggesting a more general failure of LGL-1 and LET-413 exclusion from the apical surface rather than specific invasion of the basolateral domain into the midline gaps.
evidence: Supported by Figure 5G, I showing LGL-1 and LET-413 at non-gap midline regions.

claim: The mislocalization of LGL-1 and LET-413 in PAR-6gut(-) embryos suggests a more general failure of LGL-1 and LET-413 exclusion from the apical surface rather than specific invasion of the basolateral domain into the midline gaps.
source: LGL-1 and LET-413 were also observed at midline 'non-gap' regions, where apical markers localized (Figure 5G, I insets, orange arrowheads), suggesting a more general failure of LGL-1 and LET-413 exclusion from the apical surface rather than specific invasion of the basolateral domain into the midline gaps.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of LGL-1 and LET-413 at both gap and non-gap regions.

claim: All PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae arrested as young L1 larvae.
source: Indeed, all PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae arrested as young L1 larvae (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting that intestinal function was severely compromised.
evidence: Supported by Figure 6A showing larval arrest data.

claim: Only 39% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae arrested as L1 larvae.
source: Surprisingly, only 39% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae arrested as L1 larvae.
evidence: Supported by larval arrest assay data.

claim: In 98% of control larvae, blue food traveled through and filled the entire lumen without leaking into the body.
source: In 98% of control larvae, blue food traveled through and filled the entire lumen without leaking into the body (Figure 6B, D).
evidence: Supported by Figure 6B, D showing feeding assay results.

claim: In 83% of PAR-6gut(-) larvae and 93% of PKC-3gut(-) larvae, blue food passed through the pharynx and pharyngeal valve but was trapped at the anterior end of the intestine, suggesting a luminal obstruction in the first intestinal ring (int1).
source: However, in 83% of PAR-6gut(-) larvae and 93% of PKC-3gut(-) larvae, blue food passed through the pharynx and pharyngeal valve but was trapped at the anterior end of the intestine, suggesting a luminal obstruction in the first intestinal ring (int1), which comprises the four anterior star cell daughters (Figure 6B, E, F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 6B, E, F showing feeding assay results.

claim: Blue food leaked into the body of 10% of PAR-6gut(-) and 2% of PKC-3gut(-) larvae.
source: Blue food leaked into the body of a small percentage of larvae (10% of PAR-6gut(-), 2% of PKC-3gut(-)), suggesting that most of the PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae that ingested food retained their intestinal barrier function, at least between the pharyngeal valve and int1.
evidence: Supported by feeding assay data.

claim: Most PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae that ingested food retained their intestinal barrier function, at least between the pharyngeal valve and int1.
source: Blue food leaked into the body of a small percentage of larvae (10% of PAR-6gut(-), 2% of PKC-3gut(-)), suggesting that most of the PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae that ingested food retained their intestinal barrier function, at least between the pharyngeal valve and int1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low percentage of larvae with leaked food.

claim: 42% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae had a normal intestine, 23% had an early int1 obstruction, and 20% had a more posterior obstruction.
source: Consistent with their milder larval arrest phenotype, CDC-42gut(-) larvae also showed a lower penetrance of obstructed intestines; 42% had a normal intestine (Figure 6G), 23% had an early int1 obstruction (Figure 6G'), and 20% had a more posterior obstruction.
evidence: Supported by Figure 6G, G' showing feeding assay results for CDC-42gut(-) larvae.

claim: When the star cell divisions in PAR-6gut(-) embryos were blocked with the cdc-25.2(0) mutation, a larger proportion of resulting larval intestines had a more posterior obstruction than PAR-6gut(-) larvae (25% vs. 5%).
source: When the star cell divisions in PAR-6gut(-) embryos were blocked with the cdc-25.2(0) mutation, a larger proportion of resulting larval intestines had a more posterior obstruction than PAR-6gut(-) larvae (25% vs. 5%, Figure 6B, H).
evidence: Supported by Figure 6B, H showing feeding assay results for PAR-6gut(-); cdc-25.2(0) larvae.

claim: The defects imposed by the loss of PAR-6 in the dividing star cells could be rescued by blocking the anterior star cell divisions, allowing a continuous int1/int2 connection to form more frequently.
source: These results indicate that the defects imposed by the loss of PAR-6 in the dividing star cells could be rescued by blocking the anterior star cell divisions, allowing a continuous int1/int2 connection to form more frequently.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cdc-25.2(0) rescue experiment.

claim: PAR-6 is required during elongation itself and not just during earlier intestinal development.
source: To determine if PAR-6 is required during elongation itself and not just during earlier intestinal development, we used a later promoter asp-1 to express intestinal ZIF-1 and degrade PAR-6 in 2-fold-stage embryos ('PAR-6late gut(-)'), after the star cells divided and before intestinal elongation completed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). We observed partially penetrant larval arrest (16%, Figure 6A) and obstructed lumen phenotypes (16%, Figure 6B, I, I'), consistent with a continued requirement for PAR-6 during embryonic intestinal elongation.
evidence: Supported by Figure 6A, B, I, I' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing late PAR-6 depletion results.

claim: Wild-type PKC-3 was able to rescue the larval arrest and obstructed lumen defects and restore apical PAR-6 localization in PKC-3gut(-) embryos.
source: We found that wild-type PKC-3 was able to rescue the larval arrest and obstructed lumen defects and restore apical PAR-6 localization in embryos (Figure 7A, E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, G).
evidence: Supported by Figure 7A, E, F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, G showing rescue data.

claim: The PAR-6-binding mutant PKC-3(ΔPB) showed almost no larval rescuing activity.
source: As expected, the PAR-6-binding mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity (Figure 7B, E, F), but surprisingly, embryos showed apical PAR-6 enrichment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, G).
evidence: Supported by Figure 7B, E, F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, G showing rescue data.

claim: Embryos expressing the PAR-6-binding mutant PKC-3(ΔPB) showed apical PAR-6 enrichment.
source: As expected, the PAR-6-binding mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity (Figure 7B, E, F), but surprisingly, embryos showed apical PAR-6 enrichment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, G).
evidence: Supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, G showing PAR-6 localization data.

claim: The PKC-3[G336N] kinase mutant partially rescued larval lethality and luminal obstruction and was strikingly similar to the CDC-42gut(-) phenotype.
source: The PKC-3[G336N] kinase mutant partially rescued larval lethality and luminal obstruction and was strikingly similar to the CDC-42gut(-) phenotype (Figure 7C, C', E, F); by contrast, the PKC-3[K282A] kinase mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 7C, C', E, F showing rescue data.

claim: The PKC-3[K282A] kinase mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity.
source: The PKC-3[G336N] kinase mutant partially rescued larval lethality and luminal obstruction and was strikingly similar to the CDC-42gut(-) phenotype (Figure 7C, C', E, F); by contrast, the PKC-3[K282A] kinase mutant showed almost no larval rescuing activity (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 7D–F showing rescue data.

claim: Both PKC-3 kinase mutants restored apical PAR-6 enrichment in embryos.
source: The two kinase mutants had differing levels of rescuing activity, though both restored apical PAR-6 enrichment in embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–G showing PAR-6 localization data.

claim: Apical PAR-6 localization is not sufficient to restore apical continuity and viability.
source: These results demonstrate that apical PAR-6 localization is not sufficient to restore apical continuity and viability, and that PKC-3 kinase activity and PAR-6-binding are both critical for normal PKC-3 function and for apical continuity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing that PAR-6 localization alone is not sufficient.

claim: PKC-3 kinase activity and PAR-6-binding are both critical for normal PKC-3 function and for apical continuity.
source: These results demonstrate that apical PAR-6 localization is not sufficient to restore apical continuity and viability, and that PKC-3 kinase activity and PAR-6-binding are both critical for normal PKC-3 function and for apical continuity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: The lumens of PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines frequently appeared to be pinched shut in multiple places, often with edematous swellings.
source: Unlike the continuous open lumen of control intestines (Figure 8A), the lumens of PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines frequently appeared to be pinched shut in multiple places, often with edematous swellings (Figure 8B, C, E), and PAR-6late gut(-) lumens also appeared pinched shut in one or two places in some larvae (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), consistent with a continued requirement for PAR-6 during elongation.
evidence: Supported by Figure 8B, C, E showing larval intestinal morphology.

claim: CDC-42gut(-) larvae generally had one or two points of luminal constriction, but the overall intestinal morphology was not as severely defective as in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae.
source: CDC-42gut(-) larvae generally had one or two points of luminal constriction (Figure 8D), but the overall intestinal morphology was not as severely defective as in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae.
evidence: Supported by Figure 8D showing CDC-42gut(-) larval intestinal morphology.

claim: All PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines had one or more int interface with a constricted lumen.
source: While control intestines clearly had an open lumen between int rings, PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) intestines all had one or more int interface with a constricted lumen, and CDC-42gut(-) larvae again showed a milder phenotype (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by Figure 8F showing quantification of luminal constrictions.

claim: Most PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae and 50% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae had their lumens pinched shut within int1.
source: Further, most PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) larvae and 50% of CDC-42gut(-) larvae had their lumens pinched shut within int1 (Figure 8G), consistent with the int1 obstruction and accumulation of blue-dyed food in the feeding assay and with the anterior star cell midline gaps caused by cell division.
evidence: Supported by Figure 8G showing quantification of int1 constrictions.

claim: PAR-6 and PKC-3 are essential during embryonic development to build an intestine with a continuous open lumen.
source: Thus, PAR-6 and PKC-3 are essential during embryonic development to build an intestine with a continuous open lumen.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the larval intestinal morphology data.

claim: PAR-3 localized to hollow sphere-like structures that were often separated by gaps in localization in PAR-6gut(-) larvae, unlike the continuous luminal PAR-3 in control L1 larval intestines.
source: Unlike the continuous luminal PAR-3 in control L1 larval intestines, PAR-3 localized to hollow sphere-like structures that were often separated by gaps in localization in PAR-6gut(-) larvae (Figure 9A–C), consistent with a polarized but discontinuous luminal surface.
evidence: Supported by Figure 9A–C showing PAR-3 localization in larvae.

claim: All PAR-6gut(-) larvae and some PAR-6late gut(-) larvae showed gaps in luminal ACT-5.
source: ACT-5 is strongly expressed in larval intestines and localizes to the apical brush border (MacQueen et al., 2005), and unlike the continuous luminal ACT-5 in control larvae, all PAR-6gut(-) larvae and some PAR-6late gut(-) larvae showed gaps in luminal ACT-5 (Figure 9D–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Figure 9D–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D showing ACT-5 localization in larvae, and citation to MacQueen et al., 2005.

claim: All PAR-6gut(-) larvae had DLG-1 bands that were clearly discontinuous between adjacent int rings in multiple places.
source: We also found DLG-1 localization to be defective. While control intestines contained a continuous ladder-like belt arrangement of DLG-1, all PAR-6gut(-) larvae had DLG-1 bands that were clearly discontinuous between adjacent int rings in multiple places (Figure 9G–I).
evidence: Supported by Figure 9G–I showing DLG-1 localization in larvae.

claim: In control larvae, LGL-1 was clearly excluded from apical surfaces along the midline.
source: In control larvae, LGL-1 was clearly excluded from apical surfaces along the midline, but in many PAR-6gut(-) larvae, we observed at least partial localization of LGL-1 to midline regions (Figure 9J–L), consistent with a continued failure to exclude basolateral proteins from the midline in PAR-6gut(-) larvae.
evidence: Supported by Figure 9J–L showing LGL-1 localization in larvae.

claim: In many PAR-6gut(-) larvae, at least partial localization of LGL-1 to midline regions was observed.
source: In control larvae, LGL-1 was clearly excluded from apical surfaces along the midline, but in many PAR-6gut(-) larvae, we observed at least partial localization of LGL-1 to midline regions (Figure 9J–L), consistent with a continued failure to exclude basolateral proteins from the midline in PAR-6gut(-) larvae.
evidence: Supported by Figure 9J–L showing LGL-1 localization in larvae.

claim: Early gaps in apical and junctional proteins and mislocalized basolateral proteins at the embryonic intestinal midline persist through morphogenesis, leading to larval intestines with discontinuous apical surfaces and junctions separated by midline regions where lumen formation failed to occur.
source: Together, these results suggest that early gaps in apical and junctional proteins and mislocalized basolateral proteins at the embryonic intestinal midline persist through morphogenesis, leading to larval intestines with discontinuous apical surfaces and junctions separated by midline regions where lumen formation failed to occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of persistent defects from embryo to larva.

claim: Tissue-specific protein degradation was a critical feature of this study.
source: A critical feature of this study was our tissue-specific protein degradation approach.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in the study.

claim: Ubiquitous somatic depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, or CDC-42 causes embryonic lethality and failed embryonic elongation due to skin defects.
source: Ubiquitous somatic depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, or CDC-42 causes embryonic lethality and failed embryonic elongation due to skin defects (Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Totong et al., 2007; Zilberman et al., 2017), thereby masking potential roles of these proteins in other tissues during or after elongation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Montoyo-Rosario et al., 2020; Totong et al., 2007; Zilberman et al., 2017.

claim: Using tissue-specific degradation, the study bypassed the requirement for PAR-6, PKC-3, and CDC-42 in earlier embryonic development and in other tissues and revealed the requirement for these proteins for apical and junctional continuity during intestinal morphogenesis.
source: Using tissue-specific degradation, we bypassed the requirement for these proteins in earlier embryonic development and in other tissues and revealed the requirement for PAR-6, PKC-3, and CDC-42 for apical and junctional continuity during intestinal morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's approach and findings.

claim: PAR-6 and PKC-3 are required embryonically to build a functional intestine, but seem to be dispensable once the functional intestine has been built.
source: While we found that PAR-6 and PKC-3 are required embryonically to build a functional intestine, they seem to be dispensable once the functional intestine has been built, even though intestinal elongation continues through larval development (Castiglioni et al., 2020), suggesting that the embryonic and larval intestines elongate via different mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and citation to Castiglioni et al., 2020.

claim: The embryonic and larval intestines elongate via different mechanisms.
source: While we found that PAR-6 and PKC-3 are required embryonically to build a functional intestine, they seem to be dispensable once the functional intestine has been built, even though intestinal elongation continues through larval development (Castiglioni et al., 2020), suggesting that the embryonic and larval intestines elongate via different mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential requirement for PAR-6 and PKC-3 in embryonic vs. larval stages.

claim: Dividing cells were sensitive to depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, and CDC-42 during intestinal morphogenesis.
source: Our study found that dividing cells were sensitive to depletion of PAR-6, PKC-3, and CDC-42 during intestinal morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Star cells contribute only three of the nine int rings that build the intestine, yet over half of the midline gaps in 1.5-fold embryos affected star cell daughters.
source: Star cells contribute only three of the nine int rings that build the intestine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), yet over half of the midline gaps in 1.5-fold embryos affected star cell daughters.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and gap frequency data.

claim: Cell division appears to cause the high frequency of gap formation in star cells as inhibition of the star cell divisions ameliorated the gaps caused by PAR-6 depletion.
source: Cell division appears to cause this high frequency of gap formation as inhibition of the star cell divisions ameliorated the gaps caused by PAR-6 depletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cdc-25.2(0) experiment.

claim: Apical microtubules contribute to the establishment and maintenance of apical and junctional domains.
source: Apical microtubules contribute to the establishment and maintenance of apical and junctional domains (Feldman and Priess, 2012; Harris and Peifer, 2005; Vasileva and Citi, 2018), so losing apical microtubules during mitosis could weaken the integrity of an epithelial cell and make it more dependent on the PAR complex to maintain polarity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Feldman and Priess, 2012; Harris and Peifer, 2005; Vasileva and Citi, 2018.

claim: Losing apical microtubules during mitosis could weaken the integrity of an epithelial cell and make it more dependent on the PAR complex to maintain polarity.
source: Apical microtubules contribute to the establishment and maintenance of apical and junctional domains (Feldman and Priess, 2012; Harris and Peifer, 2005; Vasileva and Citi, 2018), so losing apical microtubules during mitosis could weaken the integrity of an epithelial cell and make it more dependent on the PAR complex to maintain polarity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known role of apical microtubules.

claim: In Drosophila neuroblasts, parallel inputs from PAR complex proteins and microtubules assemble a polarized Pins/Gαi crescent to orient the mitotic spindle.
source: In Drosophila neuroblasts, parallel inputs from PAR complex proteins and microtubules assemble a polarized Pins/Gαi crescent to orient the mitotic spindle (Siegrist and Doe, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegrist and Doe, 2005.

claim: Apical microtubules and PAR-6 could redundantly maintain the apical domain in star cells; loss of the apical domain would thus only occur when both apical microtubules and PAR-6 are absent, as in dividing PAR-6gut(-) star cells.
source: Similarly, apical microtubules and PAR-6 could redundantly maintain the apical domain in star cells; loss of the apical domain would thus only occur when both apical microtubules and PAR-6 are absent, as in dividing PAR-6gut(-) star cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the analogy to Drosophila neuroblasts.

claim: Division requires the formation of new junctions between daughter cells, a process that could specifically rely on the known ability of PAR complex proteins to regulate junction formation and maturation during polarity establishment.
source: Division also requires the formation of new junctions between daughter cells (Baum and Georgiou, 2011; Roignot et al., 2013), a process that could specifically rely on the known ability of PAR complex proteins to regulate junction formation and maturation during polarity establishment.
evidence: Supported by citations to Baum and Georgiou, 2011; Roignot et al., 2013.

claim: The adherens junctions of interphase cells can promote tissue integrity in dividing neighbor cells by orienting the mitotic spindle, maintaining adhesion, and regulating the length of the new cell-cell interface.
source: The adherens junctions of interphase cells can promote tissue integrity in dividing neighbor cells by orienting the mitotic spindle, maintaining adhesion, and regulating the length of the new cell-cell interface (Gloerich et al., 2017; Herszterg et al., 2013; Higashi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gloerich et al., 2017; Herszterg et al., 2013; Higashi et al., 2016.

claim: Synchronous division of neighboring cells creates a new challenge as both cells remodel their junctions at the same time, which could temporarily remove important positional information and adhesion.
source: Synchronous division of neighboring cells therefore creates a new challenge as both cells remodel their junctions at the same time, which could temporarily remove important positional information and adhesion.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known role of junctions.

claim: When wild-type star cells divided synchronously, HMR-1 and DLG-1 levels were drastically reduced.
source: Indeed, we observed that when wild-type star cells divided synchronously, HMR-1 and DLG-1 levels were drastically reduced.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of junctional protein levels during synchronous divisions.

claim: When PAR-6gut(-) star cells divided synchronously, persistent midline gaps in the apical MTOC formed, but such gaps were not observed during asynchronous divisions.
source: In addition, when PAR-6gut(-) star cells divided synchronously, persistent midline gaps in the apical MTOC formed, but we did not observe such gaps during asynchronous divisions.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations comparing synchronous and asynchronous divisions.

claim: Either apical PAR-6 or a non-dividing neighboring cell is sufficient for new daughter cells to correctly remodel and build junctions, but loss of both can impair this remodeling.
source: These results suggest that either apical PAR-6 or a non-dividing neighboring cell is sufficient for new daughter cells to correctly remodel and build junctions, but that loss of both can impair this remodeling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synchronous vs. asynchronous division data.

claim: Adherens junctions may function as an external orientation cue to ensure correct polarity and junction position in daughter cells.
source: Thus, adherens junctions may function as an external orientation cue to ensure correct polarity and junction position in daughter cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the role of junctions in dividing cells.

claim: The midline gap phenotype in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) embryos became more severe during the greater than threefold increase in intestine length that occurred by the L1 larval stage.
source: Elongating epithelial tubes often must increase the area of the apical domains and junctions of their underlying cells, and consistently, the midline gap phenotype in PAR-6gut(-) and PKC-3gut(-) embryos became more severe during the greater than threefold increase in intestine length that occurred by the L1 larval stage.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparing embryonic and larval phenotypes.

claim: Later PAR-6 depletion in elongating intestines resulted in discontinuous lumens, albeit less frequently, suggesting a continued requirement for PAR-6 during embryonic intestine development.
source: In addition, later PAR-6 depletion in elongating intestines also resulted in discontinuous lumens, albeit less frequently, suggesting a continued requirement for PAR-6 during embryonic intestine development.
evidence: Supported by late PAR-6 depletion experiments.

claim: Most gaps occurred at interfaces between anterior and posterior cells without visible physical cell separation.
source: Most gaps occurred at interfaces between anterior and posterior cells without visible physical cell separation, raising the question of what causes cell-cell interfaces to be vulnerable to loss of PAR-6 or PKC-3.
evidence: Supported by gap location analysis.

claim: Basolateral protein localization to the midline in PAR-6gut(-) embryos was not specific to the gaps, indicating that basolateral protein localization to the midline does not create apical and junctional gaps.
source: While we observed some basolateral protein localization in the gaps in PAR-6gut(-) embryos, the signal was not specific to the gaps, indicating that basolateral protein localization to the midline does not create apical and junctional gaps.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of basolateral protein localization.

claim: Compromised apical and junctional expansion could allow basolateral proteins to diffuse into the new midline space created by elongation.
source: Alternatively, compromised apical and junctional expansion could allow basolateral proteins to diffuse into the new midline space created by elongation.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of basolateral protein mislocalization.

claim: The primary defect in PAR-6-, PKC-3-, and CDC-42-depleted intestines is a failure to maintain the coordination of apicobasal polarity between cells.
source: The primary defect in PAR-6-, PKC-3-, and CDC-42-depleted intestines is a failure to maintain the coordination of apicobasal polarity between cells; apical and junctional gaps correlated with luminal gaps in larval intestines, the luminal gaps blocked the passage of food, and young larvae arrested and died.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Apical and junctional gaps correlated with luminal gaps in larval intestines.
source: The primary defect in PAR-6-, PKC-3-, and CDC-42-depleted intestines is a failure to maintain the coordination of apicobasal polarity between cells; apical and junctional gaps correlated with luminal gaps in larval intestines, the luminal gaps blocked the passage of food, and young larvae arrested and died.
evidence: Supported by correlation between embryonic gaps and larval luminal defects.

claim: Intestines depleted of PAR-6, PKC-3, or CDC-42 rarely leaked, so barrier function appeared largely intact.
source: Intestines depleted of PAR-6, PKC-3, or CDC-42 rarely leaked, so barrier function appeared largely intact.
evidence: Supported by feeding assay data showing low leakage frequency.

claim: This result was unexpected due to the known requirement for PAR-6 in junction maturation.
source: This result was unexpected due to the known requirement for PAR-6 in junction maturation (Totong et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Totong et al., 2007.

claim: DLG-1 appeared to recover a junction-like localization in PAR-6gut(-) larvae.
source: While junctional DLG-1 localization was dim and fragmented in PAR-6gut(-) embryos (Totong et al., 2007, this study), DLG-1 appeared to recover a junction-like localization in PAR-6gut(-) larvae.
evidence: Supported by observation of DLG-1 localization in larvae and citation to Totong et al., 2007.

claim: DLG-1 was usually visibly continuous between the anterior valve and int1 in PAR-6gut(-) larvae, which may explain why their barrier function remained intact.
source: In addition, DLG-1 was usually visibly continuous between the anterior valve and int1, which may explain why their barrier function remained intact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of DLG-1 continuity.

claim: A secondary mechanism may drive later septate-like junction formation independent of PAR-6 and PKC-3.
source: This result suggests that a secondary mechanism may drive later septate-like junction formation independent of PAR-6 and PKC-3.
evidence: This is speculation based on the recovery of DLG-1 localization.

claim: The transmembrane Crumbs polarity complex is a critical polarity regulator in many epithelia.
source: A candidate parallel pathway is the transmembrane Crumbs polarity complex, a critical polarity regulator in many epithelia (Charrier et al., 2015; Tepass et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Charrier et al., 2015; Tepass et al., 1990.

claim: Simultaneous removal of all three C. elegans Crumbs homologs does not cause obvious polarity defects.
